Theory: how sommer parameterizes and optimizes covariance structures

sommer development team

2026-09-26

Source: vignettes/sommer.theory.Rmd
sommer.theory.Rmd

This vignette is written like a short book. Each chapter builds on the previous one, and all chapters share the same notation so formulas can be compared directly across chapters:

  • θ\theta : a natural parameter — a variance, a correlation, a range — the thing that has a real statistical meaning but also has to obey a rule (e.g. “must be positive”).
  • η\eta : a working parameter — the same information, but recoded so it is allowed to be any real number, with no rule to break.
  • gg : the transform connecting them, θ=g(η)\theta = g(\eta).
  • K(η)K(\eta) : the (dimensionless) covariance shape, normalized so K11=1K_{11}=1.
  • σ2\sigma^2 : the single overall scale, owned by vsm().
  • Λ=K−1\Lambda = K^{-1} : the precision (inverse covariance shape).
  • Bk=∂K/∂ηkB_k = \partial K/\partial \eta_k : the structural derivative of the shape with respect to working parameter kk.

Chapter 1: The linear mixed model and Henderson’s equations

1.1 The model 

mmes(fixed = y ~ 1, random = ~ vsm(...), rcov = ~ vsm(...), data = ...)

fits

y=Xβ+∑i=1rZiui+e,ui∼N(0,Gi),e∼N(0,R) y = X\beta + \sum_{i=1}^{r} Z_i u_i + e, \qquad u_i \sim N(0, G_i), \quad e \sim N(0, R)

  • β\beta: fixed effects.
  • uiu_i: random effects, one term per random=~... entry.
  • Gi=var(ui)G_i = \mathrm{var}(u_i), R=var(e)R = \mathrm{var}(e): the covariance matrices this whole vignette is about.

sommer never treats GiG_i or RR as free unconstrained matrices. Every one is built from a small number of variance components θ\theta (Chapter 2), and REML estimates θ\theta, not the matrix entries directly.

1.2 Henderson’s Mixed Model Equations (MME)

Rather than maximizing the marginal likelihood of yy directly (which needs V=ZGZ′+RV = ZGZ' + R, generally dense and huge), Henderson’s equations solve for β,u\beta,u jointly using only R−1R^{-1} and Gi−1G_i^{-1}:

C(β̂û)=(X′R−1yZ′R−1y),C=(X′R−1XX′R−1ZZ′R−1XZ′R−1Z+G−1) C\begin{pmatrix}\hat\beta\\ \hat u\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}X'R^{-1}y\\ Z'R^{-1}y\end{pmatrix}, \qquad C = \begin{pmatrix} X'R^{-1}X & X'R^{-1}Z\\ Z'R^{-1}X & Z'R^{-1}Z + G^{-1} \end{pmatrix}

with G−1=blockdiag(G1−1,…,Gr−1)G^{-1} = \mathrm{blockdiag}(G_1^{-1}, \dots, G_r^{-1}).

Why this matters for parameterization: every quantity sommer actually needs — CC, its log-determinant, and the REML score/AI-matrix — is built from inverses (R−1R^{-1}, Gi−1G_i^{-1}) and their derivatives with respect to θ\theta, never from GiG_i or RR themselves except to invert them once per structure per iteration. This is why sommer’s internal name for Gi−1G_i^{-1} within a structure is Lambda (Λ=K−1\Lambda = K^{-1}).

1.3 Where covariance structures come in

For a random term built with vsm(dsm(Env), usm(Trait), ism(Line)), sommer constructs

G=σ2⋅Kdsm⊗Kusm⊗Kism G = \sigma^2 \cdot K_{dsm} \otimes K_{usm} \otimes K_{ism}

  • Exactly one free scale σ2\sigma^2 per vsm() call (its sigma2 argument).
  • Every other factor (dsm, usm, ism, …) supplies a dimensionless shape KK with K11=1K_{11}=1.

This separation of scale (one parameter, always variance-like) from shape (any number of parameters, some variance-like, some correlation-like) is the central design decision explored in the rest of this vignette, and it directly determines how derivatives are computed in ai_mme_sp2().

1.4 Preview of the key distinction (developed in Chapter 4)

Variance-type parameter Correlation-type parameter
Example sigma2, dsm() ratios, fam() specific variances csm()/ar1m() rho, usm()/corgm() off-diagonal terms
Effect on KK rescales one or few diagonal blocks reshapes the entire matrix jointly
Bk=∂K/∂ηkB_k=\partial K/\partial \eta_k sparse / diagonal dense
Average vs Expected Information typically agree closely can diverge — needs EM/AI blending
Practical consequence fast trace/derivative shortcuts available full dense chain-rule required

Chapter 2: Parameterization theory, explained from first principles

2.1 Why we can’t just let the computer search freely

Imagine you are tuning two dials for a model:

  • Dial A controls a variance. It must always stay strictly positive — a “negative amount of variability” makes no sense.
  • Dial B controls a correlation. It must always stay strictly between −1-1 and 11 — a correlation of 22 or −3-3 makes no sense either.

If you let an optimization algorithm (the computer’s “hill-climbing” procedure that tries to improve the fit step by step) move these dials by any amount, in any direction, it will sooner or later try an illegal value: a negative variance, or a correlation bigger than 1. At that point the model is broken (the covariance matrix stops being a valid one — technically it is no longer positive definite, which is the mathematical way of saying “this could actually occur as a covariance of real data”).

sommer’s answer to this problem is always the same trick, used for every single covariance structure in the package:

Never let the optimizer touch the real dial (θ\theta). Instead, give it a fake dial (η\eta) that can be turned all the way in either direction, forever, without ever breaking anything. Then use a fixed recipe (gg) to translate the fake dial’s position into a legal value of the real dial.

Formally: θ=g(η)\theta = g(\eta), where η\eta ranges over all real numbers (−∞-\infty to ∞\infty) and gg is built so that g(η)g(\eta)always lands in the legal range for θ\theta, no matter what η\eta is.

This is exactly the same idea used elsewhere in statistics: for example, when you model a probability (which must stay in [0,1][0,1]) with a logistic regression, you don’t optimize the probability directly — you optimize an unconstrained “logit” score and convert it to a probability at the very end. sommer does the same thing, systematically, for every variance and correlation in every covariance structure it supports.

2.2 The working-parameter vector

In sommer’s code, the collection of fake dials for one covariance structure is called par (short for “working parameters”), and it always lives in the CovarianceFactor descriptor returned by every constructor (csm(), ar1m(), usm(), …). Three related pieces travel together:

  • par — the current numeric values of η\eta.
  • free — a logical flag per entry: is this ηk\eta_k estimated by REML, or is the user holding it fixed (fixed=TRUE)?
  • par_names — a human-readable label per entry, e.g. "rho" or "variance_ratio[B]", used when you call summary() on a fitted model.

REML (Chapter 4) works entirely with par/η\eta. It never sees θ\theta directly; θ=g(η)\theta = g(\eta) is only computed when sommer needs to actually build the covariance matrix KK, or when it reports results back to you in a human-readable form.

2.3 Transform family 1 — variances: the exponential map

The rule: θ>0\theta > 0.

The recipe: θ=exp(η)=eη\theta = \exp(\eta) = e^{\eta}.

Why this works: no matter what real number η\eta is — very negative, zero, very positive — eηe^\eta is always a positive number. As η→−∞\eta\to-\infty, θ→0\theta\to 0 (but never reaches it); as η→+∞\eta\to+\infty, θ→∞\theta\to\infty. Every positive number is reachable by exactly one η\eta (the inverse recipe is η=log(θ)\eta=\log(\theta)).

A nice bonus: the “speed” at which θ\theta changes as you nudge η\eta (its derivative, ∂θ/∂η=eη=θ\partial\theta/\partial\eta = e^\eta = \theta) is proportional to θ\theta itself. This means equal steps in η\eta-space are equal-percentage steps in θ\theta-space (multiplicative, like moving up a musical scale in octaves) rather than equal-amount steps — exactly the natural way variances tend to move (a variance going from 1 to 2 “feels” like the same size change as going from 10 to 20).

sommer almost never applies this to a raw variance, though. Instead it applies it to a ratio relative to a reference level — this detail matters because of scale confounding (see 2.6), so let’s define it now since you will see it in almost every structure in Chapter 3:

ηj=log(θjθ1),j=2,…,q \eta_j = \log\!\left(\frac{\theta_j}{\theta_1}\right), \quad j=2,\dots,q

Level 1 is always the reference: θ1\theta_1 is fixed at 1 by definition, so only q−1q-1 working parameters are needed to describe qq relative variances.

2.4 Transform family 2 — bounded quantities: logit and tanh

The rule: θ∈(lo,hi)\theta \in (lo, hi), a bounded open interval — e.g. a correlation ρ∈(−1,1)\rho\in(-1,1), or a compound-symmetry ρ∈(−1/(q−1),1)\rho\in(-1/(q-1), 1).

The recipe (general bounded interval):

θ=lo+(hi−lo)⋅s(η),s(η)=11+e−η(the logistic/"sigmoid" function) \theta = lo + (hi-lo)\cdot s(\eta), \qquad s(\eta) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}} \ \ (\text{the logistic/"sigmoid" function})

The sigmoid function s(η)s(\eta) is the same S-shaped curve used in logistic regression: it always outputs a number strictly between 0 and 1, approaching 0 as η→−∞\eta\to-\infty and approaching 1 as η→+∞\eta\to+\infty, and it is smooth and increasing everywhere. Stretching and shifting its output (lo+(hi−lo)⋅s(η)lo + (hi-lo)\cdot s(\eta)) maps it onto any open interval (lo,hi)(lo,hi) instead of just (0,1)(0,1).

The recipe (symmetric interval (−1,1)(-1,1)): when the bounds are exactly −1-1 and 11 (as for a plain correlation), sommer often uses the equivalent but more compact hyperbolic tangent:

θ=tanh(η)=eη−e−ηeη+e−η \theta = \tanh(\eta) = \frac{e^{\eta}-e^{-\eta}}{e^{\eta}+e^{-\eta}}

which is just the logit recipe above rescaled — same S-shape, same guarantee (tanh(η)\tanh(\eta) is always strictly between −1-1 and 11), just centered at 0 instead of at 1/21/2.

Why bother with a whole interval instead of just “positive,” like variances? Because a correlation has two walls (an upper and a lower limit), while a variance only has one (a floor at 0, no ceiling). The sigmoid/tanh family is the natural tool whenever there are two walls to respect simultaneously.

A subtlety that matters in Chapter 4: near the middle of the interval, s(η)s(\eta) changes quickly as η\eta moves — a small step in η\eta makes a decent-sized change in θ\theta. But near the two walls (as η\eta gets very large in either direction), s(η)s(\eta) becomes almost flat: huge changes in η\eta barely move θ\theta at all. This is deliberate and useful — it means that if REML tries to push a correlation toward its boundary, the working scale automatically resists further movement (the “gas pedal” stops doing much once you’re already flooring it), rather than needing an artificial rule bolted on afterward.

2.5 Transform family 3 — many correlated quantities at once (factorizations)

Families 1 and 2 work great for a single variance or a single correlation, one dial at a time. But some structures have many correlations that all have to be jointly consistent with each other — for example, an unstructured 3×33\times 3 correlation matrix has 3 pairwise correlations, but not every combination of 3 numbers in (−1,1)(-1,1) is a valid correlation matrix (try ρ12=0.9,ρ13=0.9,ρ23=−0.9\rho_{12}=0.9,\ \rho_{13}=0.9,\ \rho_{23}=-0.9 — no data set can ever produce that).

So instead of transforming each correlation separately, sommer reparameterizes the whole matrix at once through a factorization — a recipe that builds the matrix out of simpler unconstrained ingredients in such a way that the result is automatically valid, no matter what those ingredients are. The two building blocks used throughout the package are:

  • Cholesky factor: any covariance/correlation matrix KK can be written as K=LL′K = LL' for some lower-triangular matrix LL with positive diagonal. Conversely, any lower-triangular LL with positive diagonal, multiplied by its own transpose, automatically produces a valid (positive definite) K=LL′K = LL' — there is no combination of entries of LL that can break this. So sommer parameterizes LL instead of KK: the off-diagonal entries of LL are unconstrained working parameters directly, and the diagonal entries of LL go through the family-1 exponential recipe (to keep them positive). Used by usm() (Chapter 3.7) and, restricted to unit-diagonal LL, by corgm() (Chapter 3.8).
  • Loadings + diagonal (“factor-analytic”) factor: K∝ΛΛ′+ΨK \propto \Lambda \Lambda' + \Psi for a rectangular loading matrix Λ\Lambda (any real numbers) and a diagonal matrix Ψ\Psi with positive entries (again via the family-1 recipe). A sum of “something squared” (ΛΛ′\Lambda\Lambda', always positive semi-definite) and “something positive on the diagonal” (Ψ\Psi) is always positive definite — again, automatically, for any real Λ\Lambda. Used by fam()/rrcm() (Chapter 3.9) and, in a triangular/banded variant, by antem() (Chapter 3.10).

The common thread across all three families: every recipe in this chapter is a one-way-safe translation from “any real number(s) at all” to “a legal θ\theta/KK.” This is why sommer’s optimizer (Chapter 4) can take a Newton step of any size, in any direction, in η\eta-space, and never produce an invalid model — the only thing that can still go wrong is that the fit gets worse, which is a completely different (and much easier to handle) problem than breaking the math.

2.6 Why the reference level matters: avoiding scale confounding

Recall from Chapter 1 that a vsm() term is a Kronecker product G=σ2⋅K1⊗K2⊗⋯G = \sigma^2\cdot K_1\otimes K_2\otimes\cdots. If every KiK_i were allowed to carry its own free overall scale (instead of being pinned to Ki,11=1K_{i,11}=1 via a reference level), the model would have infinitely many (σ2,K1,K2,…)(\sigma^2, K_1,K_2,\dots) combinations that produce the exact same GG — for instance doubling σ2\sigma^2 while halving every entry of K1K_1 changes nothing observable. This is called non-identifiability: REML would have no way to choose among the infinitely many equally-good answers, and the optimizer would wander aimlessly or fail to converge.

sommer avoids this by a strict convention, applied without exception: every covariance-shaping factor is normalized so its first diagonal entry is exactly 1 (K11=1K_{11}=1), and the one and only free overall scale lives in vsm()’s sigma2 argument. This is why, throughout Chapter 3, you will see “θ1\theta_1 is the reference, fixed at 1” repeated for structure after structure — it is not a coincidence, it is the mechanism that keeps the whole model identifiable.

Chapter 3: Catalog of covariance structures

For each structure: the shape formula K(η)K(\eta) (normalized so K11=1K_{11}=1), the working parameters η\eta and their transform (from Chapter 2), and whether it is fundamentally a variance-type or correlation/shape-type parameterization (this label is used again in Chapter 4 and in the matching worked example of Chapter 5).

3.1 ism(x) — identity

K=Iq,no free parameters.K = I_q, \qquad \text{no free parameters.}

Simplest possible shape: independent, homoscedastic levels. Used as the “main effect” incidence in most vsm() calls, or as a Kronecker factor when no structure is desired on one dimension.

3.2 dsm(x, values, fixed, theta) / atm(x, levs, values, fixed) — heterogeneous diagonal variances

K=diag(1,θ2/θ1,…,θq/θ1),ηj=log(θj/θ1),j=2,…,q K = \mathrm{diag}(1, \theta_2/\theta_1, \dots, \theta_q/\theta_1), \qquad \eta_j = \log(\theta_j/\theta_1),\ j=2,\dots,q

Family-1 (exponential/log-ratio) transform, applied to every level except the reference. Pure variance-type structure: q−1q-1 free log-variance ratios, no correlation at all (off-diagonal is exactly 0). atm() is the same construction restricted to a user-selected subset of levels (levs); unselected levels get zero columns in the design matrix and are excluded from η\eta.

3.3 csm(x, rho, fixed, variance, values) — compound symmetry

Kii=1,Kij=ρ(i≠j),lo=−1q−1<ρ<1 K_{ii}=1,\quad K_{ij}=\rho\ (i\neq j), \qquad lo=\frac{-1}{q-1} < \rho < 1

Family-2 (bounded logit) transform: ηρ=logit(ρ−lo1−lo)\eta_\rho = \mathrm{logit}\!\left( \frac{\rho-lo}{1-lo}\right).

  • variance="homogeneous" (default): only ηρ\eta_\rho is free — a single correlation-type parameter.
  • variance="heterogeneous": additionally appends q−1q-1 family-1 log-variance-ratios ηj=log(θj/θ1)\eta_j=\log(\theta_j/\theta_1), so K=diag(θ)Rdiag(θ)K=\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt\theta)\, R\, \mathrm{diag}(\sqrt\theta) with RR the homogeneous compound-symmetric correlation. A mixed parameterization: 1 correlation-type + (q−1)(q-1) variance-type parameters.

3.4 ar1m/ar2m/ar3m/toeplitzm — autoregressive & general Toeplitz correlation

All parameterize an ordered correlation matrix through partial autocorrelations (PACF) κ∈(−1,1)order\kappa\in(-1,1)^{order}, family-2 (tanh) transform η=atanh(κ)\eta=\mathrm{atanh}(\kappa), reconstructed to full correlations ρh\rho_h (lag hh) via the Durbin–Levinson recursion:

Kij=ρ|i−j| K_{ij} = \rho_{|i-j|}

  • ar1m(): order 1, ρh=ρh\rho_h=\rho^h (the classical AR(1) correlation), 1 correlation-type parameter.
  • ar2m()/ar3m(): order 2/3, PACF vector of length 2/3 mapped through Durbin–Levinson to ρh\rho_h for all lags up to q−1q-1.
  • toeplitzm(): order q−1q-1 (fully general stationary Toeplitz correlation, no autoregressive-order restriction) — the most flexible member of this family, still guaranteed valid for any PACF in (−1,1)q−1(-1,1)^{q-1} (this is exactly the joint-validity guarantee discussed in Chapter 2.5, achieved here through PACF rather than through a matrix factorization).
  • All four support variance = "heterogeneous" (AR family only; toeplitzm() is shape-only) the same way as csm(): append q−1q-1 family-1 log-variance-ratios after the PACF working parameters.

3.5 mam/ma1m/ma2m — moving-average covariance

K∝Cov(et+θ1et−1+θ2et−2) K \propto \mathrm{Cov}\!\left(e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1} + \theta_2 e_{t-2}\right)

Working parameters are the raw MA coefficients themselves (η=θ\eta=\theta, no transform at all) — unlike AR, any finite MA coefficients produce a valid covariance; invertibility of the MA polynomial is not required to define the covariance matrix, so no bounding transform is needed. This is the one “ordered” structure whose working parameter equals its natural parameter directly. Purely a correlation/shape-type structure (no variance option).

3.6 corgm(x, theta, fixed) — general correlation matrix

K=AA′,A unit-diagonal lower-triangular(Aii=1) K = AA', \qquad A \text{ unit-diagonal lower-triangular} \ (A_{ii}=1)

Family-3 (factorization) transform: the strictly-lower-triangular entries of AA are working parameters directly (no further per-entry transform is needed — Chapter 2.5 explains why any real lower-triangular AA with unit diagonal automatically gives a valid KK). q(q−1)/2q(q-1)/2 purely correlation-type parameters, no variance component at all (contrast with usm() below, which also carries diagonal/variance information).

3.7 usm(x, theta, fixed) — general unstructured covariance

K=LL′,L lower-triangular,L11=1 K = LL', \qquad L \text{ lower-triangular}, L_{11}=1

Family-3 (Cholesky factorization) transform: for each free entry of LL below the diagonal — the off-diagonal entries are working parameters directly (η=Lij\eta=L_{ij}), the diagonal entries go through the family-1 log transform (η=logLii\eta=\log L_{ii}, keeping Lii>0L_{ii}>0 hence KK nonsingular). Total q(q+1)/2−1q(q+1)/2 - 1 free parameters (the −1-1 is L11=1L_{11}=1, fixed by the Chapter 2.6 reference-level convention).

This is the maximally flexible valid shape for qq levels — every possible covariance shape is reachable, at the cost of O(q2)O(q^2) parameters. It mixes variance-type (log-diagonal) and correlation-type (off-diagonal) working parameters in a single structure.

3.8 fam(x, k, loadings, specific, fixed) / rrcm(x, k, loadings, fixed) — factor-analytic covariance

M=ΛΛ′+Ψ,K=M/M11 M = \Lambda\Lambda' + \Psi, \qquad K = M / M_{11}

Family-3 (loadings + diagonal) transform:

  • Λ\Lambda: q×kq\times k loadings, lower-triangular in its leading k×kk\times k block (for a unique, “rotationally identified” solution), diagonal entries family-1 log-parameterized (must be positive by convention), off-diagonal loadings unconstrained working parameters.
  • Ψ=diag(ψ1,…,ψq)\Psi=\mathrm{diag}(\psi_1,\dots,\psi_q): specific variances, family-1 parameterized as q−1q-1 log-ratios relative to ψ1\psi_1 (the reference level, per Chapter 2.6).

A rank-kkcorrelation-type structure (loadings) plus a genuinely variance-type component (specific variances) — a compact alternative to usm() when qq is large and a low-rank + diagonal approximation is statistically reasonable (the standard “FA” model for many traits or many environments). rrcm() is the same loading parameterization with Ψ=I\Psi=I fixed (a pure reduced-rank approximation, no free specific variances) — purely correlation/shape-type.

3.9 antem(x, order, beta, innovations, fixed) — antedependence

Ty=e,Cov(e)=D diagonal,K=T−1DT−T,D11=1 Ty = e,\quad \mathrm{Cov}(e)=D \text{ diagonal},\qquad K = T^{-1} D T^{-T},\quad D_{11}=1

TT is unit lower-triangular with regression coefficients βij\beta_{ij} only in the requested order subdiagonals (working parameters = β\beta directly, unconstrained — a banded relative of the family-3 factorization idea). DD’s remaining diagonal entries are q−1q-1 family-1 log-innovation-ratios (variance-type). A mixed structure like usm() but banded/order-limited rather than fully dense, useful for longitudinal/repeated-measures data where dependence should decay with temporal order but need not follow a strict AR form.

3.10 maternm(x, range, nu, fixed, distance) — Matérn spatial correlation

Kij=21−νΓ(ν)(2νdijr)νKν(2νdijr) K_{ij} = \frac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)} \left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu}\,d_{ij}}{r}\right)^{\!\nu} K_\nu\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu}\,d_{ij}}{r}\right)

Family-1 (log) transform on both parameters: η=(logr,logν)\eta = (\log r, \log \nu) (both must be positive: range and smoothness). Distance dijd_{ij} comes from supplied coordinates or a user-supplied distance matrix. Two correlation-type (in the “shape” sense — they reshape the whole matrix, not just rescale one entry) parameters governing decay rate and smoothness of spatial dependence.

3.11 sar(x, W, rho, fixed) — simultaneous autoregressive spatial covariance

B=I−ρW,M=B−1B−T,K=M/M11 B = I - \rho W, \qquad M = B^{-1}B^{-T}, \qquad K = M/M_{11}

Family-2 (bounded logit) transform: ρ\rho bounded by the inverse spectral radius of WW (guarantees BB nonsingular). One correlation-type (shape) parameter that reshapes the entire spatial covariance through matrix inversion.

3.12 car(x, W, rho, fixed) — proper conditional autoregressive covariance

Q=D−ρW,D=diag(rowSums(W)),M=Q−1,K=M/M11 Q = D-\rho W,\quad D=\mathrm{diag}(\text{rowSums}(W)),\qquad M=Q^{-1},\qquad K=M/M_{11}

Family-2 (bounded logit) transform: ρ\rho bounded by the reciprocal extreme eigenvalues of the normalized adjacency S=D−1/2WD−1/2S=D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2} (the exact condition for QQ to stay valid). Same flavor as sar(): one correlation/shape-type parameter, whole-matrix reshaping via inversion.

3.13 ownm(x, K, fun, par, fixed, dfun) — user-defined shape

Either a fixed known valid matrix K (zero free parameters, sommer only normalizes it by its [1,1][1,1] entry), or a user function fun(par) returning a valid matrix, normalized the same way. Here the user is responsible for choosing their own transform family from Chapter 2 (or inventing a new one); sommer only imposes the final K11=1K_{11}=1 normalization. If dfun(par,k) (analytic Bk=∂K/∂ηkB_k=\partial K/\partial\eta_k) is not supplied, ai_mme_sp2() falls back to a numerical derivative. This is the escape hatch for any structure not already covered — it plugs into the exact same CovarianceFactor interface as maternm()/toeplitzm()/sar()/car().

3.14 covm(ran1, ran2, thetaC, theta, ...) — legacy two-random-effect helper

Predates the general vsm() Kronecker interface; builds a CovarianceFactor directly from two random-effect terms and an explicit correlation-structure matrix thetaC/theta. Internally normalized and compiled through the same descriptor contract as every structure above, so it participates in REML identically once compiled — retained mainly for backward compatibility with older model specifications.

Chapter 4: REML, AI-REML, and ai_mme_sp2()

4.1 The REML log-likelihood sommer maximizes

For the Henderson system of Chapter 1, the (restricted) log-likelihood ai_mme_sp2() evaluates every iteration is

ℓ(η)=−12(log|C|+log|R|+∑inilog|Ai|+y′Py) \ell(\eta) = -\tfrac12\Big( \log|C| \;+\; \log|R| \;+\; \sum_i n_i\log|A_i| \;+\; y'Py \Big)

mapped directly onto the code:

  • logDetC — log|C|\log|C|, from the sparse Cholesky/LDLT factorization of Henderson’s CC matrix (or CHOLMOD/PCG-approximated for large sparse CC).
  • logDetR — log|R|\log|R|, computed per residual-structure branch (diagonal fast path, Kronecker-residual branch, or dense fallback).
  • logDetA(i) — −log|Ai−1|-\log|A_i^{-1}| per random effect (relationship/precision matrices), via sparse LDLT.
  • yPy — the quadratic form y′Pyy'Py from absorbing yy into the MME solve.

REML maximizes ℓ(η)\ell(\eta) over the working parameters η\eta from Chapter 2 (not the natural parameters θ\theta), using a Newton-type Average-Information (AI) REML algorithm.

4.2 The AI-REML update

η(t+1)=η(t)+InfMat−1s(η(t)) \eta^{(t+1)} = \eta^{(t)} + \mathrm{InfMat}^{-1}\, s(\eta^{(t)})

  • s(η)s(\eta): the score vector, ∂ℓ/∂η\partial\ell/\partial\eta.
  • InfMat: a convex blend of the Average Information matrix (avInf) and the Expected Information matrix (emInf):
InfMat = (weightAiInfMat * avInf) + (weightEmInfMat * emInf);

with per-iteration weights (emweight/weightEmInf, user/schedule controlled) trading off AI-REML’s fast quadratic convergence against classical EM-REML’s guaranteed monotone ascent and better global behavior when the AI matrix is momentarily ill-conditioned. This blending is exactly the mechanism that absorbs the numerical differences between variance-type and correlation-type parameters described below — when the AI block for a dense correlation structure is poorly conditioned, increasing the EM weight locally stabilizes the step without touching the well-behaved variance blocks.

4.3 The core object: precision and its derivative

For a covariance shape K(η)K(\eta), sommer works with its inverse (precision) Λ=K−1\Lambda = K^{-1} (lambdaDense in ai_mme_sp2()). All REML derivatives route through the standard matrix-inverse identity:

∂Λ∂ηk=−ΛBkΛ,Bk=∂K∂ηk \frac{\partial \Lambda}{\partial \eta_k} = -\Lambda B_k \Lambda, \qquad B_k = \frac{\partial K}{\partial \eta_k}

implemented essentially verbatim:

arma::mat dLambda = -lambdaDense * Bk * lambdaDense;   // Bk = dK/d(eta_k)
dLambda = 0.5 * (dLambda + dLambda.t());               // symmetrize (roundoff)

Bk (called cachedCovarianceD1()/covarianceD1() in the code) is where every structure-specific formula from Chapter 3 actually enters the optimizer — for analytic structures (diag, AR, CSM, US, …) it’s a closed-form matrix; for generic-interface structures (maternm, toeplitzm, sar, car, ownm without dfun) it’s a numerical derivative of the R-level evaluator function. Either way, from this point on ai_mme_sp2() treats Bk identically regardless of structure — the only thing that changes the downstream numerics is what Bk looks like, which is precisely the variance-vs-correlation distinction below.

4.4 Variance-type parameters: sparse/diagonal BkB_k

For a pure variance-ratio working parameter (e.g. dsm()’s ηj=log(θj/θ1)\eta_j=\log(\theta_j/\theta_1), or vsm()’s own outer sigma2):

K=diag(1,θ2/θ1,…),Bj=∂K∂ηj=θj/θ1⋅ejej′ K = \mathrm{diag}(1,\theta_2/\theta_1,\dots),\qquad B_j = \frac{\partial K}{\partial \eta_j} = \theta_j/\theta_1 \cdot e_j e_j'

BkB_k is rank-one and diagonal — a single nonzero entry. Consequences:

  • dΛk=−ΛBkΛ\mathrm{d}\Lambda_k = -\Lambda B_k \Lambda collapses to a rank-one update restricted to row/column jj: cheap to form, cheap to multiply against other quantities.
  • The trace terms needed for the score and for avInf/emInf (generically tr(PdCk)\mathrm{tr}(P\,\mathrm{d}C_k) and tr(PdCiPdCj)\mathrm{tr}(P\,\mathrm{d}C_i\,P\,\mathrm{d}C_j)) reduce to a small number of scalar row/column contractions instead of full dense matrix products — this is exactly the “diagonal residual fast path” specialization used for pure-variance residual structures, which only exists because the derivative itself is diagonal, not because the covariance is diagonal per se.
  • For the single overall sigma2 in vsm(), ∂G/∂σ2=K\partial G/\partial\sigma^2 = K exactly (the whole shape, undifferentiated) — the classical textbook variance-component REML derivative. This is the parameter for which Average Information and Expected Information coincide most closely in well-behaved models, which is part of why classical variance-components REML (pre-AI, EM-only) worked well for decades on models built purely from ism()/dsm()-type structures.

4.5 Correlation-type parameters: dense BkB_k

For a correlation/shape working parameter (e.g. csm()’s ηρ=logit(⋅)\eta_\rho=\mathrm{logit}(\cdot), ar1m()’s η=atanh(ρ)\eta=\mathrm{atanh}(\rho), usm()/corgm()’s Cholesky-factor entries):

∂K∂ηρ=∂K∂ρ⋅∂ρ∂ηρ \frac{\partial K}{\partial \eta_\rho} = \frac{\partial K}{\partial \rho}\cdot\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial \eta_\rho}

Both factors are dense in general: changing a single correlation parameter perturbs every off-diagonal entry of KK simultaneously (e.g. for ar1m(), Kij=ρ|i−j|K_{ij}=\rho^{|i-j|} so ∂Kij/∂ρ=|i−j|ρ|i−j|−1\partial K_{ij}/\partial\rho = |i-j|\,\rho^{|i-j|-1} is nonzero for every i≠ji\neq j). Consequences:

  • BkB_k is a full q×qq\times q matrix with no exploitable sparsity in general (compound symmetry and AR have some exploitable structure, but not the sparsity a diagonal derivative gives).
  • dΛk=−ΛBkΛ\mathrm{d}\Lambda_k=-\Lambda B_k\Lambda is a genuinely dense matrix product, O(q3)O(q^3) per parameter per iteration — no shortcut analogous to the diagonal case.
  • The chain-rule factor ∂ρ/∂ηρ\partial\rho/\partial\eta_\rho (derivative of the logit-inverse or tanh\tanh from Chapter 2.4) is itself not constant: for the bounded-logit map, ∂ρ/∂η=(1−lo)⋅s(1−s)\partial\rho/\partial\eta = (1-lo)\cdot s(1-s) where s=logit−1(η)s=\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\eta), which vanishes as η→±∞\eta\to\pm\infty (i.e. as ρ\rho approaches its boundary). This is the same “flattening near the walls” property described in Chapter 2.4 — it naturally damps REML steps that would otherwise push ρ\rho against its feasible limit — but it also means the information matrix entries for correlation parameters shrink near the boundary, unlike variance parameters, whose exponential-family Jacobian never vanishes (only grows as θ\theta grows).
  • Because dense BkB_k products couple every pair (i,k)(i,k) of structure parameters through tr(PdCiPdCj)\mathrm{tr}(P\,\mathrm{d}C_i\,P\,\mathrm{d}C_j), the resulting avInf block for correlation parameters is fully dense and more prone to near-singularity (e.g. when a correlation parameter is weakly identified, or two correlation parameters trade off against each other, as in usm() with many levels and modest sample size) — this is precisely the situation the EM/AI blending in Section 4.2 exists to stabilize: emInf (expected information) is guaranteed valid and typically better conditioned than avInf in these dense/boundary-adjacent regimes, so increasing its weight recovers a well-defined, descent-guaranteeing step even when avInf alone would not.

4.6 trust_cap: a second REML-stability mechanism tied to parameter type

Independent of AI/EM blending, ai_mme_sp2() also enforces a per-parameter trust-region cap (trust_cap in each CovarianceFactor) that bounds how far a single working parameter may move in one iteration:

arma::vec caps = Rcpp::as<arma::vec>(f["trust_cap"]);
  • Variance-type parameters (unbounded exponential map) are typically given a larger cap — sigma2-like parameters can safely take large multiplicative steps early in REML with little risk of overshoot causing invalidity — only the likelihood itself, not validity, is at stake.
  • Correlation-type / bounded-map parameters (e.g. maternm()’s range/nu use c(1.0, 0.75), sar()/car() use 1.0) are given tighter caps, because a large step on the working scale, pushed through a saturating transform (logit/tanh), can still correspond to a huge change in the reconstructed matrix’s conditioning even though the value itself stays valid — the cap prevents a technically-valid but wildly-overshooting proposal from destabilizing the next likelihood evaluation.

This is a purely numerical safeguard layered on top of the always-valid-by-construction guarantee from Chapter 2 — validity is never at risk, but good conditioning and monotone likelihood ascent are, and they are protected differently for the two parameter families.

4.7 Summary: the full chain per parameter type 

flowchart TD
    A["Working parameter eta (unconstrained, R)"] -->|transform g| B["Natural parameter theta (variance / correlation)"]
    B -->|reconstruction formula| C["Covariance shape K(eta)"]
    C -->|invert| D["Precision Lambda = K^-1"]
    D -->|analytic identity dLambda = -Lambda Bk Lambda| E["dLambda/d(eta_k)"]
    E --> F["Score s(eta), avInf, emInf"]
    F -->|blend + trust_cap| G["AI-REML Newton step"]
    G --> A
Stage Variance-type parameter Correlation-type parameter
Transform (Ch. 2) family 1: exponential (unbounded above) family 2/3: logit/tanh/factorization (saturating, bounded)
Bk=∂K/∂ηkB_k = \partial K/\partial \eta_k sparse/diagonal, rank-1 dense, full matrix
Cost of dΛk\mathrm{d}\Lambda_k cheap (structured update) O(q3)O(q^3) dense product
avInf conditioning usually well-behaved can be near-singular, especially near boundary or weak identifiability
EM/AI blend role rarely needed often needed for stability
trust_cap looser tighter

This is the concrete, code-level answer to “how does the REML process differ between a variance parameter and a correlation parameter”: both are optimized by the same AI-REML machinery over unconstrained working parameters (Chapter 2), but the structure of their derivative (BkB_k, hence dΛk\mathrm{d}\Lambda_k, hence the AI/EM information blocks) is fundamentally sparser and better-conditioned for variance parameters than for correlation parameters, which is why sommer layers EM/AI blending and per-parameter trust caps on top of a uniform derivative framework rather than hard-coding structure-specific optimizers.

Chapter 5: Worked examples, one per structure

Every example below reuses the exact notation from Chapter 2 (θ\theta, η\eta, gg, KK, σ2\sigma^2, Λ\Lambda, BkB_k) so you can trace each structure’s entry in Chapter 3 all the way to a concrete number.

5.1 ism()

q=2q=2 levels, no working parameters at all: K=I2=(1001)K=I_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1 \end{pmatrix}, Λ=K−1=I2\Lambda = K^{-1} = I_2. There is no η\eta to iterate on for this factor — it contributes only through the Kronecker product with the other factors in the same vsm() term.

5.2 dsm()

q=3q=3 levels, natural variances θ=(1,2.25,0.81)\theta=(1, 2.25, 0.81) (already showing θ1=1\theta_1=1, the reference from Chapter 2.6). Family-1 transform:

η2=log(2.25/1)=0.8109,η3=log(0.81/1)=−0.2107 \eta_2=\log(2.25/1)=0.8109,\qquad \eta_3=\log(0.81/1)=-0.2107

K=diag(1,2.25,0.81),Λ=K−1=diag(1,0.4444,1.2346) K=\mathrm{diag}(1,\ 2.25,\ 0.81),\qquad \Lambda = K^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(1,\ 0.4444,\ 1.2346)

q=3q=3, lo=−1/(q−1)=−0.5lo=-1/(q-1)=-0.5. Suppose ρ=0.4\rho=0.4. Family-2 transform:

5.4 csm(), heterogeneous

Same ρ=0.4\rho=0.4 (ηρ=0.4055\eta_\rho=0.4055), plus variances θ=(1,1.5,0.6)\theta=(1,\ 1.5,\ 0.6) giving η2=log(1.5)=0.4055\eta_2=\log(1.5)=0.4055, η3=log(0.6)=−0.5108\eta_3=\log(0.6)=-0.5108 (family-1, exactly as in 5.2). Full working vector: η=(0.4055,0.4055,−0.5108)\eta=(0.4055,\ 0.4055,\ -0.5108) — 1 correlation-type entry followed by 2 variance-type entries, the “mixed” row of the Chapter 3.15 table.

5.5 ar1m()

q=4q=4, ρ=0.5\rho=0.5. Family-2 (tanh) transform: η=atanh(0.5)=0.5493\eta=\mathrm{atanh}(0.5)= 0.5493.

K=(10.50.250.1250.510.50.250.250.510.50.1250.250.51) K=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 & 0.25 & 0.125\\ 0.5 & 1 & 0.5 & 0.25\\ 0.25 & 0.5 & 1 & 0.5\\ 0.125 & 0.25 & 0.5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}

Kij=ρ|i−j|K_{ij}=\rho^{|i-j|}; the single working parameter reshapes every off-diagonal band simultaneously (dense B1B_1, Chapter 4.5).

5.6 ar2m() / ar3m() / toeplitzm()

q=4q=4, order-2 PACF κ=(0.3,−0.2)\kappa=(0.3,-0.2). Family-2 transform: η=(atanh(0.3),atanh(−0.2))=(0.3095,−0.2027)\eta=(\mathrm{atanh}(0.3), \mathrm{atanh}(-0.2)) = (0.3095,\ -0.2027). The Durbin–Levinson recursion (Chapter 3.4) turns κ\kappa into full lag correlations ρ1,ρ2,ρ3\rho_1,\rho_2,\rho_3, which then fill Kij=ρ|i−j|K_{ij}=\rho_{|i-j|} exactly like ar1m() above but allowing a richer decay pattern. toeplitzm() with q=4q=4 would use 3 PACF values (one per lag up to q−1q-1) instead of being capped at a fixed AR order.

The resulting KK is built from Cov(et+θ1et−1)\mathrm{Cov}(e_t+\theta_1 e_{t-1}), giving a banded correlation matrix with only lag-1 correlation nonzero. Chapter 6: End-to-end numerical trace, from η\eta to the REML objective

Chapters 2-5 showed how a working parameter η\eta turns into a shape KK and a precision Λ\Lambda. This chapter shows where in the computation those numbers actually get used, by carrying one tiny, fully-numeric example all the way from η\eta to the REML log-likelihood ℓ(η)\ell(\eta) itself — reusing the exact usm() numbers from Section 5.8.

6.1 A 4-observation, 2-line x 2-trait toy data set

Two lines (L1,L2L_1,L_2), two traits (A,BA,B), one observation per line-trait combination, model y=𝟏β+u+ey=\mathbf{1}\beta + u + e (a single fixed intercept β\beta, one random effect per line-trait cell, and residual noise). Take the random-effect design as vsm(usm(Trait), ism(Line)), which makes each line’s 2-vector of trait effects ul=(ul,A,ul,B)u_{l}=(u_{l,A},u_{l,B}) independent across lines with common covariance σ2K\sigma^2 K:

y=(101289)(order: L1A,L1B,L2A,L2B),X=(1111),Z=I4,R=I4 y = \begin{pmatrix}10\\12\\8\\9\end{pmatrix}\ \ (\text{order: } L_1A,\ L_1B,\ L_2A,\ L_2B), \qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=I_4,\qquad R=I_4

To isolate exactly what the shape working parameters do, fix the scale at σ2=1\sigma^2=1 and the residual variance at 11 (in a real mmes() fit these would be extra variance-type working parameters of their own, following Section 4.4).

6.2 Step 1 — working parameters to the shape and its precision (Chapter 2-3)

Exactly the Section 5.8 usm() example: η=(η21,η22)=(0.30,log0.95)\eta=(\eta_{21},\eta_{22}) = (0.30,\ \log 0.95), so L21=0.30L_{21}=0.30, L22=0.95L_{22}=0.95, and

K=(1.00000.30000.30000.9925),Λ=K−1=(1.0997−0.3324−0.33241.1080) K=\begin{pmatrix}1.0000&0.3000\\0.3000&0.9925\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Lambda=K^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1.0997&-0.3324\\-0.3324&1.1080\end{pmatrix}

6.3 Step 2 — precision to Henderson’s CC matrix (Chapter 1)

Because lines are independent (ism(Line)), the random-effect precision G−1=σ−2(I2⊗Λ)G^{-1}=\sigma^{-2}\,(I_2\otimes\Lambda) is block-diagonal, one copy of Λ\Lambda per line — this is literally the only place η\eta enters the whole computation; every quantity from here on is arithmetic built on top of these four numbers. Henderson’s CC (Section 1.2), with R=I4R=I_4 so Z′R−1Z=I4Z'R^{-1}Z=I_4:

C=(4111112.0997−0.3324001−0.33242.1080001002.0997−0.3324100−0.33242.1080) C=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1&1&1&1\\ 1 & 2.0997&-0.3324&0&0\\ 1 & -0.3324&2.1080&0&0\\ 1 & 0&0&2.0997&-0.3324\\ 1 & 0&0&-0.3324&2.1080 \end{pmatrix}

rows/columns ordered (β,uL1A,uL1B,uL2A,uL2B)(\beta,\,u_{L_1A},\,u_{L_1B},\,u_{L_2A},\,u_{L_2B}). The Λ\Lambda blocks sit exactly where Z′R−1ZZ'R^{-1}Z would otherwise be left alone — η\eta’s only job, computationally, is to determine these four numbers added into CC.

6.4 Step 3 — solving the MME (BLUEs/BLUPs depend on η\eta)

Solving C(β̂,û)′=(X′R−1y,Z′R−1y)′=(39,10,12,8,9)′C\,(\hat\beta,\hat u)' = (X'R^{-1}y,\ Z'R^{-1}y)' = (39,\,10,\,12,\,8,\,9)' gives

β̂≈9.752,ûL1A≈0.294,ûL1B≈1.113,ûL2A≈−0.914,ûL2B≈−0.501 \hat\beta \approx 9.752,\quad \hat u_{L_1A}\approx 0.294,\ \hat u_{L_1B}\approx 1.113,\quad \hat u_{L_2A}\approx -0.914,\ \hat u_{L_2B}\approx -0.501

If η\eta had been different, Λ\Lambda would differ, the four numbers inserted in Section 6.3 would differ, and every one of these five solutions would come out different — this is the concrete meaning of “the BLUPs/BLUEs depend on the covariance parameters.”

6.5 Step 4 — from the MME solution to the REML ingredients (Chapter 4.1)

Using the identity y′Py=y′R−1y−(X′R−1y,Z′R−1y)⋅(β̂,û)y'Py = y'R^{-1}y - (X'R^{-1}y,\,Z'R^{-1}y)\cdot(\hat\beta,\hat u):

y′R−1y=102+122+82+92=389,y′Py≈389−384.81≈4.19 y'R^{-1}y = 10^2+12^2+8^2+9^2 = 389, \qquad y'Py \approx 389 - 384.81 \approx 4.19

and, from the same CC matrix of Section 6.3 (a block-determinant calculation, done in practice by sparse Cholesky, not shown here step by step),

log|C|≈3.48 \log|C| \approx 3.48

With ism(Line) contributing log|A−1|=0\log|A^{-1}|=0 and R=I4R=I_4 contributing log|R|=0\log|R|=0, Chapter 4.1’s REML log-likelihood becomes a single concrete number:

ℓ(η)=−12(log|C|+log|R|+∑inilog|Ai|+y′Py)≈−12(3.48+0+0+4.19)≈−3.83 \ell(\eta) = -\tfrac12\big(\log|C| + \log|R| + \textstyle\sum_i n_i\log|A_i| + y'Py\big) \approx -\tfrac12(3.48+0+0+4.19) \approx -3.83

This is the number AI-REML is trying to make as large as possible, and every term in it was produced starting from the two numbers in η\eta.

6.6 Step 5 — perturbing η\eta: where the score/AI-matrix machinery lives

Section 4.3 gives the analytic derivative ∂Λ/∂ηk=−ΛBkΛ\partial\Lambda/\partial\eta_k = -\Lambda B_k\Lambda. We can check this numerically instead of trusting the formula blindly, using the same finite- difference idea a high-school calculus class would use for any derivative: nudge η21\eta_{21} from 0.300.30 to 0.310.31 (holding η22\eta_{22} fixed), rebuild KK and Λ\Lambda exactly as in Section 6.2, and see how much Λ\Lambda moved.

Nudged value: L21=0.31,L22=0.95L_{21}=0.31,\ L_{22}=0.95, giving K22=0.312+0.952=0.9986K_{22}=0.31^2+0.95^2=0.9986 (note detK=(L11L22)2=0.9025\det K = (L_{11}L_{22})^2=0.9025 is unchanged, since only the off-diagonal η21\eta_{21} moved) and

Λnudged≈(1.1064−0.3435−0.34351.1080) \Lambda_{\text{nudged}} \approx \begin{pmatrix}1.1064&-0.3435\\-0.3435&1.1080\end{pmatrix}

Finite-difference estimate of the derivative:

Λnudged−Λ0.01≈(0.668−1.108−1.1080.000) \frac{\Lambda_{\text{nudged}}-\Lambda}{0.01} \approx \begin{pmatrix}0.668&-1.108\\-1.108&0.000\end{pmatrix}

Compare this to the analytic formula from Section 4.3/5.8, B1=∂K/∂η21=(0110.60)B_1=\partial K/\partial\eta_{21}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0.60\end{pmatrix}, plugged into −ΛB1Λ-\Lambda B_1 \Lambda:

−ΛB1Λ≈(0.665−1.108−1.1080.000) -\Lambda B_1 \Lambda \approx \begin{pmatrix}0.665&-1.108\\-1.108&0.000\end{pmatrix}

The two match (up to the expected finite-step-size rounding). This is exactly the object ai_mme_sp2() forms internally as dLambda (Section 4.3), and it is what turns into the score s(η)s(\eta) and the avInf/emInf blocks of Section 4.2 that decide the next value of η\eta — closing the loop: η→K→Λ→C→(β̂,û)→ℓ(η)\eta \to K \to \Lambda \to C \to (\hat\beta,\hat u) \to \ell(\eta) for the forward pass (Sections 6.2-6.5), and η→Bk→dΛk→s(η),InfMat→η(t+1)\eta \to B_k \to \mathrm{d}\Lambda_k \to s(\eta),\,\mathrm{InfMat} \to \eta^{(t+1)} for the update that drives REML to convergence (Chapter 4.2).

Where to go from here

  • To fit a model with any of these structures, see ?vsm and the constructor’s own help page (e.g. ?csm, ?ar1m, ?usm).
  • For the descriptor-level API details (fields of a CovarianceFactor, free, par_names, trust_cap), see using-covariance-structures.Rmd.
  • For a deeper look at the specific performance optimizations inside ai_mme_sp2() referenced in Chapter 4 (sparse LDLT, CHOLMOD, PCG, selected-inverse traces), see the package’s C++ source comments in src/MNR.cpp.
